lesson.title: Possessives Agree with the Thing
lesson.subtitle: mi, tu, su, mis, tus, sus — possessives agree with the possession, not the owner

hook.title: Look at the Possession, Not the Owner!
hook.content: In English, you choose 'his' or 'her' by looking at the owner ('Paul's mother' = his mother; 'María's book' = her book). In Spanish, possessives look forward at the THING OWNED! Mi ('my'), tu ('your', informal — no accent!), and su ('his, her, its, your-formal, or their') only change for SINGULAR vs PLURAL: mi libro → mis libros, tu amigo → tus amigos, su casa → sus casas! Meanwhile, nuestro ('our') changes for both gender and number: nuestro padre, nuestra madre, nuestros amigos, nuestras casas.

pattern.title: Unaccented 'tu' ('your') vs Accented 'tú' ('you')
pattern.content: Here is why written accents matter so much in Spanish: tú (with an accent) is the subject pronoun 'you' (Tú tienes), while tu (without an accent) is the possessive 'your' (tu casa 'your house')!
pattern.linguist_note: Latin meus, tuus, suus reduced in proclitic position to mi, tu, su before nouns.
pattern.trap_note: Never write an accent on possessive tu ('your': tu libro) or mi ('my': mi casa). Accented tú means 'you' and accented mí means 'me' after a preposition (para mí)!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: mi, tu, su, nuestro, el padre, la madre
exercises.meaning: my (singular / plural: mis), your (informal, no accent! / plural: tus), his, her, your-formal, their (plural: sus), our (nuestro / nuestra / nuestros / nuestras), father (plural los padres = parents), mother
exercises.explanation: mi/tu/su add -s for plural possessions (mis/tus/sus); nuestro agrees in both gender and number.

exercises.prompt: Spanish hermano ('brother', hermana 'sister') comes from Latin frāter germānus ('full/genuine brother'). Which English adjective meaning 'closely relevant or belonging to the same family of ideas' is its exact twin?
exercises.meaning: something 'germane' to a topic belongs to the same nuclear family!
exercises.explanation: Latin germānus ('of the same parents/seed') gave English germane and Spanish hermano.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'my friends' in Spanish?
exercises.explanation: Because amigos is plural, mi adds -s: mis amigos.
la familia is feminine singular, so nuestro becomes nuestra: Nuestra familia es grande.

exercises.idea: ask a friend where their house is: 'Where is your house?'
exercises.explanation: ¿Dónde está tu casa? — unaccented tu means 'your'.

diagnosis.cue: tú with a tilde means 'you'; unaccented tu means 'your': tu casa.

summary.outcome: Match mi/mis, tu/tus, su/sus in number and nuestro/a/os/as in gender and number with the possession.

use_example.german: Mi padre, mi madre y mis hermanos viven en nuestra casa.
use_example.english: My father, my mother, and my siblings live in our house.

summary.takeaway: mi, tu, and su care only whether the possession is singular or plural; nuestro cares about gender too.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([1401] Singular vs Plural Possessions): drill mi/mis, tu/tus, and nuestro/nuestra across family and objects.

twist.explanation: Son mis amigos — plural verb son + plural mis amigos.

foreshadow.line: You just unlocked the Sentence Gate! In Topic 15, we count from 1 to 100 and discover why Spanish expresses age and hunger with tener.

payoff.text: In Topic 13 you saw para mí ('for me', with an accent); now you see why unstressed mi ('my', no accent) omits the tilde!

mi.shift_rule: Agrees in number with the possession
mi.context_phrase: Es mi amigo y ellos son mis amigos.
mi.context_translation: He is my friend and they are my friends.
mi.etymology_derivation: Unstressed mi (no accent) means 'my'; accented mí (after a preposition: para mí) means 'me'!

tu_poss.shift_rule: No accent on possessive tu ('your') vs. accented tú ('you')

su.english_meaning: his, her, its, your (usted), their (plural: sus)
su.shift_rule: Agrees in number with the thing owned (su / sus)
su.context_translation: María is looking for her brother.
su.etymology_derivation: Only changes for singular (su libro) vs. plural (sus libros) — never for gender!

nuestro.english_meaning: our (agrees in gender and number: nuestro/a/os/as)
nuestro.etymology_derivation: Unlike mi/tu/su, nuestro agrees in both gender and number: nuestro padre, nuestra madre.

padre.etymology_derivation: Plural los padres means 'the parents' (mother and father together).

hermano.context_phrase: Tengo un hermano y una hermana.
hermano.context_translation: I have a brother and a sister.
hermano.etymology_derivation: Latin germānus ('of the same seed/parents', English 'germane') lost its initial g- in Spanish: hermano!

casa.etymology_derivation: Latin casa originally meant a cottage, replacing domus in everyday Romance speech.
